2027-07-15.title: Saint Bonaventure, Bishop and Doctor of the Church
readings: I AM has sent me to you
Remember the wonderful works he has done
Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest
2027-07-15.alt: Memorial of St Bonaventure (white). The Lectionary gives no proper readings, so the readings of Thursday of the Fifteenth Week (Year I) are used. Psalm 105 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and in the NRSV. The memorial of St Bonaventure is kept on 15 July, the day he died. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-15.verse: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
theo: Moses has met God at the burning bush and been sent to Egypt, and now he asks a practical question: “If I come to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your ancestors has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” In the ancient world a name was not a label; it opened a person's character and a way into a relationship. God answers with the most mysterious sentence in the Old Testament: “I am who I am.” The Hebrew, ehyeh asher ehyeh, can mean “I am who I am,” or “I will be who I will be,” or “I will be there as who I will be”: the God who simply is, and who is present and faithful. Then God gives a shorter form that Israel would speak with great reverence, the divine Name written with four Hebrew letters (YHWH), which our Bibles print as “the Lord” in capitals, and which pious Jews never pronounce out of respect. The Church has the same reverence and does not pronounce it in worship. “This is my name forever, and this my title for all generations.” Notice that the name comes joined to a history: “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob.” God is not an idea; he is the God of a family and a promise. Moses is to gather the elders and say: “I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt.” The God who is is the God who looks. He also tells the truth about the road ahead: “the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.” The liberation will be costly and slow, but God says plainly: “I will stretch out my hand.” The psalm answers with thanksgiving for what he has done: “Remember the wonderful works he has done, his miracles,” and especially that he “sent his servant Moses, and Aaron whom he had chosen.”

From the mountain of God we go to the lake of Galilee, and to words of rest. After the reproach of the towns and the thanksgiving of Jesus, there is this invitation: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.” The people who heard him knew about burdens: the labour of poor farmers and fishermen, taxes, and a religion that some teachers had loaded with many rules. In Jewish teaching “the yoke” was a familiar picture for the study and keeping of the Law and for the service of God; Ben Sira had said: “Put your neck under her yoke, and let your souls receive instruction.” Jesus takes up the picture and changes it: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.” He does not abolish the yoke; he offers his own, which is himself. A yoke was usually worn by two animals together, so to take his yoke is to be joined to him and to walk at his side. And the teacher is not a hard master: “I am gentle and humble in heart.” Learning from Jesus means learning meekness, and rest is the fruit: “you will find rest for your souls.” This is the sentence that echoes Jeremiah's “ancient paths,” where Israel was told to “find rest for your souls.” His yoke is “easy” because love makes burdens light, and because he carries it with us. The Exodus reading and the Gospel fit: the God who says “I am” has come to the weary, and the Son who knows the Father invites everyone to come.
outline: Ask: what burden are you carrying that nobody knows about?
Point 1 · I am who I am
God gives Moses his name, and the name is joined to faithfulness.
Point 2 · I have seen, and I will stretch out my hand
The God who looks, and tells the truth about the road.
The easy yoke of Jesus, gentle and humble of heart.
Point 4 · St Bonaventure, the Seraphic Doctor
Learning that ends in love, and a heart set on the Crucified.
“Come to me … and I will give you rest.”
live: Make the Sign of the Cross slowly today, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and let it be a prayer, not a habit.
Name your heaviest burden to Jesus in a few words tonight, and say: I take your yoke; carry this with me. Ask also whom you can help to carry theirs.
saints: Born in Bagnoregio in Italy, he joined the Franciscans and studied and taught in Paris, where he was a contemporary of St Thomas Aquinas. A story tells that as a child he was healed through the prayers of St Francis; when his mother later told Francis, he is said to have exclaimed: “O buona ventura!” (good fortune). He became Minister General of the Order in 1257 and wrote the Life of St Francis and the Journey of the Mind into God, a guide from creatures to the cross and to God. Named cardinal bishop of Albano, he died during the Council of Lyons on 15 July 1274. Pope Sixtus V declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1588; he is called the Seraphic Doctor.
2027-07-15.prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you told Moses your name and you promised to be with your people. Teach us to say your name with love and reverence, and to trust that you have seen what is done to us. Lord Jesus, gentle and humble of heart, we are weary and burdened: we come to you. Take your yoke upon us, and carry it with us, and give us rest. As you gave St Bonaventure a mind enlightened by learning and a heart on fire with love for the Crucified, give us a faith that studies, adores and serves. Amen.
altar: The Mass is the place where the weary come. “Come to me,” says Jesus, and in the Eucharist we come to him: the priest holds up the bread and says, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and we answer, “Lord, I am not worthy.” We lay down the burden of the week and receive his rest. St Bonaventure loved the Eucharist, and he taught that every study of God must end in love, adoration and thanksgiving, which the Mass makes real in the sacrifice of Christ.

quick: Moses asks God's name; God answers “I am who I am,” and joins his Name to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
God has seen the misery in Egypt, promises liberation, and warns that Pharaoh will let the people go only when compelled by a mighty hand.
Jesus invites all who are weary and burdened to come to him, and offers his easy yoke: he is gentle and humble in heart.
2027-07-15.action: Say to Jesus tonight what is weighing on you most, and ask him to carry it with you.
2027-07-15.question: Whom do I trust to carry my burdens, and how willingly do I let Jesus take his share?
kidsaint: Bonaventure was a little boy in Italy who became very ill. His mother prayed to St Francis, and the boy got better. Many years later, a story says, Francis remembered and said: O buona ventura, good fortune! That is how Bonaventure may have got his name. He grew up to join the Franciscan brothers, became a famous teacher and was made a cardinal. He wrote the story of St Francis and taught that studying is not enough: we must love Jesus with all our hearts.

family.explain: Jesus says: Come to me, all you who are tired and carry heavy loads, and I will give you rest. He is gentle and kind, and he never makes us feel small. A yoke is a wooden bar that two oxen wear on their shoulders so they can pull a plough together. Jesus says: wear my yoke, and I will walk with you! If something is too heavy for you to carry alone, you can give it to Jesus. He will carry it with you.
family.intention: We pray for everyone who is tired or worried, and we thank Jesus for walking beside us.
family.ask: Ask: “What is a worry or a heavy thing that each of us can give to Jesus tonight?”

illus: A farmer near Palakkad once showed a visitor how two bullocks are yoked for ploughing. One was young and strong, the other old and slow. The visitor asked why the farmer put them together, and the farmer smiled. The young one takes most of the weight, he said, and the old one learns to keep the line straight. Neither of them could do the field alone. The visitor remembered it years later when he read Jesus' words about his yoke, and he thought that this is a picture of how Jesus walks with us: we are the slow one, and he takes most of the weight. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you are who you are, and you are with us. Lord Jesus, gentle and humble of heart, give us rest. Amen.
share: I am who I am (Exodus 3:14). What does it mean to me that God simply is, always there and always faithful?
I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you (Exodus 3:16). When did I feel that God had seen my trouble?
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me (Matthew 11:29). What would it look like to walk with Jesus in the way I deal with my burdens?
pm.resp: Remember the wonderful works he has done.
interc: For the Church, that she may always be a place of rest for the weary and the burdened.
For the Franciscan family and for all who teach theology and the faith, that learning may lead to love.
For those who carry heavy burdens in secret: illness, debts, a broken family, fear for the future.
For peoples who are oppressed and are crying out for justice and dignity, that God's mighty hand may be seen among them.
For our group, that we may take the yoke of Jesus willingly and learn gentleness from him.
pm.close: Father, you revealed your name to Moses and your heart in your Son. Give rest to the weary and make us gentle and humble in heart, like Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Moses asks a very honest question: what is his name? He is afraid that when he goes to Egypt the people will ask, and he will have no answer. And God says: I am who I am (Exodus 3:14). It is the most mysterious of all answers. God does not say: I am the strongest, or the greatest. He says: I am. I am here, I am faithful, I am the one who is. And he adds: the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob. His name is joined to the names of a family and a promise.

And listen to what God says next: I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt (Exodus 3:16). He has seen. Whoever is suffering today should hear this first: God has seen. And he tells the truth: the king will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand (Exodus 3:19). The road will be hard. But God says: I will stretch out my hand. He does not promise an easy road; he promises himself.

And now Jesus, in the Gospel, says almost the same thing in the language of a friend: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). Who is weary today? Come. Who carries a burden? Come. Not first to an idea or a rule, but to him. And what does he give? Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29). The yoke of two. We do not pull alone.

St Bonaventure, whom we remember today, was one of the most learned men of the Middle Ages, and yet he said that learning must end in love. He had a mind like a library and a heart like a flame, and the flame was fed by the Crucified. Let us do the same: let us study, let us pray, and let us come to the Lord and put our burden on his shoulder. Amen.
kids: Children, Moses asked God: what is your name? And God said: I am. That means: I am always here for you. Then Jesus says to us: Come to me, all who are tired and sad, and I will give you rest. He says: I am kind and gentle. When something is too heavy for you, you can give it to Jesus, like giving your school bag to a big brother to carry! St Bonaventure was a very clever teacher who loved Jesus very much. He taught that the most important thing is to love. Let us tell Jesus today what is heavy for us.
